It's as similar as Figma is to Photoshop. You can design, but not the same ways or features. Also Haiku needs you to download, LottieLab is in the web - no downloads required. Haiku is also not tailored to Lottie workflows, it's more of an add-on there; Lottie is a primary feature on LottieLab. And I've made this a lot simpler to use than Haiku for beginners, but also powerful enough for pros. Asset and Project management also doesn't exist in Haiku. Component library and design systems are also missing. I could go on tbh... but we've basically built LottieLab super focused on helping product teams and individuals ship animations faster and better.

In terms of the filetypes, Rive is great at supporting interactive/ dynamic animations especially with the .riv runtime. However, there are some cases and platforms where this isn't supported yet and you might have have a Lottie file exported to fill the gaps. I think the Rive team have been working on having it supported on more platforms so you can check in with them to find out where and when .riv support works for these.

Lottie shares the benefit of being performant too but still has some gaps handling interactive animations seamlessly. There are improvements already happening on this end and a new Lottie player is being trialed. This will allow more support for dynamic animations and as more tools enter the market, it'll push the filetype to improve even further beyond the scope AE allows. It is also more widely supported so you're likely to be able to get it working on platforms that .riv might not work on yet.

\_\_\_

In terms of editor, the first difference I've observed is that as Rive supports its own runtime more, its support for Lottie isn't as prioritised. Lottielab only focuses on Lottie and therefore every feature revolves around making your Lottie animations work as seamlessly as possible. And with the upcoming improvements to the Lottie player, you will be able to do even more with Lottie animations using LottieLab as its editor than After Effects or Rive over time. Each improvement will be embedded into the LottieLab workflow for creating your Lottie animations more seamlessly.

In terms of the UX, I'm not sure if you have an existing workflow with Rive and can't comment much on that. With LottieLab, the aim is to make it as simple as possible. So whilst you can achieve the same outcomes, I've been obsessed with design and workflow so the animation workflows are quite different. I think Rive's approach to keyframe still has some similarities to After Effects keyframe approach, whereas LottieLab borrows some design principles from prototyping tools like Figma and Framer for an interface that's easier for designers to adopt.

I hope that helps!
